description: Computer engineering students from Sulaimani turning NASA data into interactive web experiences. We build fast, design clean, and tell stories with code. Join us if you can code, design, or present!
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, bilingual web app that introduces school-age children to the NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Kids explore real Moon and Mars maps, where each object sits at its real coordinates. They tap a lander, rover, reflector or parachute, and the machine tells its own story in the first person: what it did, what it discovered and what happened to it.

The demo includes 22 objects, 11 on the Moon and 11 on Mars, from Ranger 7 (1964) to the Ingenuity helicopter. A timeline shows the hardware arriving from 1964 to today. Quizzes earn badges, stories can be narrated aloud, and a “planned vs. real life” bar shows, for example, that Opportunity lasted 57 times longer than planned.

The app is built entirely on NASA open data: Solar System Treks map tiles, the NASA Image and Video Library API, the NSSDCA Master Catalog, and LROC and HiRISE orbital imagery.

The stories behind this hardware usually sit in technical catalogs written for experts. Our app turns them into characters children can connect with, in English and Kurdish (Sorani). It’s free, runs in any browser, and new objects take minutes to add.
details:
What it does and how it works
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, bilingual web app that introduces school-age children to the NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Users switch between two real planetary maps built from NASA Solar System Treks tiles. Each piece of hardware is a glowing marker at its real coordinates. Tapping one opens a story card where the machine speaks in the first person: Ranger 7 describes photographing the Moon until impact, the Apollo 15 rover explains being the first car driven on another world, and Opportunity tells how it was built for 90 days but explored for almost 15 years. Each card also has “What I helped discover," a “Did you know?” fact, a live photo from the NASA Image and Video Library, links to NASA sources, and a short quiz. The demo covers 22 objects: 11 on the Moon and 11 on Mars, including landers, rovers, laser reflectors, deliberate impactors, lost missions, and landing leftovers such as parachutes and the sky crane.

Benefits and intended impact
The stories behind this hardware usually sit in technical catalogs written for experts. Our app turns them into characters children can connect with, so they learn the science through narrative instead of memorizing facts. Quizzes and badges encourage active recall. Because everything works in English and Kurdish (Sorani), children in Kurdistan can explore space science in their own language, where such resources are rare. The app is free, needs no installation, and runs in any browser, so it can be used at home or in classrooms. Our next step is to test it with children in local schools.

Creativity
Instead of presenting hardware as a list of specifications, we gave each machine a voice and a personality. A timeline lets children press play and watch hardware arrive year by year from 1964 to today. A “planned vs. real life” bar makes ideas like “57 times longer than planned” visual. We also included failures and debris, such as the Mars Polar Lander and Perseverance’s parachute, to show that space exploration includes setbacks and leftovers and that engineers learn from both.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, in a single self-contained page
  • Maps: Leaflet.js
  • Built-in browser features: Web Speech API for narration, Canvas for an offline fallback map
  • NASA data: Solar System Treks WMTS, the NASA Image and Video Library API, the NSSDCA Master Catalog, and LROC and HiRISE orbital imagery
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages
  • AI assistance: We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, draft text, and translate. Our team directed the concept, reviewed facts against NASA sources, and proofread and tested everything.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: Short sentences, a friendly first-person voice, large tap targets, and a mobile-friendly layout for children.
  • Accuracy: Every fact links back to a NASA source, and every object is placed at its real coordinates.
  • Language: A full Kurdish interface with right-to-left layout, not just translated labels.
  • Accessibility: It works offline with an illustrated fallback map and needs no account or installation.
  • Scalability: Each object is one entry in a data file, so new hardware can be added in minutes.
